newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Fierce exchanges rock Brazzaville after dark.
newsitem.headline: Fierce exchanges rock Brazzaville after dark.

text.p: Fierce exchanges rocked parts of the Congo Republic capital Brazzaville after dark on Wednesday.
Residents and eyewitnesses said the exchanges, which lit the night sky, appeared near the international airport and the city centre.

The firing followed a day of relative calm punctuated by sporadic bursts of gunfire -- a recent pattern in a showdown between President Pascal Lissouba and his predecessor Denis Sassou Nguesso dating back to June 5.
The exchanges followed the first parliament meetings -- both the senate and the national assembly -- of the crisis.

Legislators, who helped broker a solution to similar political and ethnic clashes that killed at least 2,000 people after disputed parliamentary elections in 1993, had been unable to meet earlier because of shelling around parliament.

In New York, U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun told Reuters that he intended to ask the Security Council to endorse an African peacekeeping force for Congo Brazzaville, paid for by the group's wealthier members.
Earlier, France and the United States joined forces to press for an end to the crisis which has killed hundreds of people, many of them civilians caught in cross-fire and indiscriminate shelling.

The French Foreign Ministry announced the joint approach in Paris earlier as Brazzaville enjoyed a relative lull in fighting, two days after Gabon's mediating president Omar Bongo sent the warring parties a fresh appeal for peace.

"France and the United States have begun a joint approach to the warring parties in Congo to convince them to pursue negotiations through the international mediators' committee chaired by Omar Bongo and cease hostilities without delay," French Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said.
He was speaking after talks in Paris on Tuesday between U.S. ambassador to Congo Aubrey Hooks and the head of the ministry's director for African affairs Jean-Didier Roisin.

Diplomats in the Democratic Republic of the Congo capital Kinshasa, across the Congo River from Brazzaville, said the next step was likely to be meetings between national mediator Bernard Kolelas, the mayor of Brazzaville and Lissouba and separately with rival Sassou, but no time had been set.
The fighting flared on June 5 when Lissouba tried to disarm Sassou's militia, ahead of presidential elections that had been due on July 27 but are now effectively postponed.
Bongo sent his latest proposals to the two protagonists on Monday, diplomats said.
Bongo, who is married to one of Sassou's daughters and is a long-standing friend of Lissouba, began his mediation three weeks ago but it has produced scant results.
Both Sassou and Lissouba say they want elections but disagree on how they can be held fairly.
The battle lines have changed little in recent days.
The southern Bacongo quarter, which is under the control of Kolelas and his militia, remains neutral and home to thousands of residents displaced from other parts of town.
A U.N. security adviser said the area around the city centre frontline was a no-man's land.
